stories.headline: Republican pushback on the Russia waiver widens, and Zelenskyy tells lawmakers the Starlink disruption continues
stories.dek: Speaker Mike Johnson urged the White House to weigh the "unintended consequences," according to Roll Call, as Ukraine's Republican allies in the House point to the lame-duck agenda and a discharge petition.
whatsNew: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said on Fox News' "Sunday Morning Futures" on Oct. 18 that there are concerns in House panels such as Intelligence and Foreign Affairs about the waiver, according to Roll Call. [[c3]] He said he had told White House officials that "we need to talk about it and I think carefully consider the unintended consequences that may ensue." [[c4]] "Congress voted on this decisively just several weeks ago, and we understand that Putin cannot be trusted," Johnson said, according to Roll Call; the New York Post also quotes him saying "we understand that Putin cannot be trusted." [[c5]]

On the same Sunday, Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) said on CBS's "Face the Nation" that "capitulating to a bully generally means they're going to make more demands going forward." [[c6]] Rep. Michael T. McCaul (R-Texas), a former chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, urged Trump to reconsider: "Time and again, we have seen how Putin responds to American concessions: with contempt for the United States and increased violence against innocent Ukrainians," CBS News reported. [[c24]] On Monday, Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) told reporters she was "extremely surprised" by the waiver and that the law "was an act of Congress that we had worked with the White House on," according to Roll Call. [[c22]] Rep. Craig A. Goldman (R-Texas) said he "would be in favor of keeping those sanctions on Russia until the war is over." [[c23]]

House Republicans who back Ukraine are now pointing to the floor and to the budget. Rep. Brian K. Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) wrote on X on Monday that the United States "must not import a single drop of Russian oil," that sanctions must be "harsher and stronger than they've ever been before," and that "each and every one of these items will be brought to the House Floor," according to Roll Call. [[c19]] He had said on Oct. 10 that a measure imposing an energy embargo on Russia "will be forced to the Floor via discharge and it will pass overwhelmingly." [[c20]] Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) wrote on Oct. 16 that "the president is prolonging the war, not ending it." [[c16]]

The second thread is Ukraine's satellite link. On Monday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told members of Congress on a video call that the disruption of Starlink services is continuing, according to Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), who hosted the call with Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.). [[c9]] Roll Call puts the number of participants at nearly two dozen members from both parties. [[c10]] According to the two senators, Zelenskyy also reported disruptions to U.S. intelligence sharing on early warning of Russian ballistic missile launches and raised concerns about interceptor delays and the sanctions waiver, CBS News reported. [[c11]] "Trying to appease a murderous thug like Vladimir Putin will only prolong this war and bring greater casualties," Tillis and Blumenthal said. [[c12]]

Rep. Michael R. Turner (R-Ohio) called on "Face the Nation" on Oct. 18 for a congressional investigation into the Starlink disruption in Ukraine. [[c7]] "There needs to be an investigation, we need to find out who these people are because lives are at risk and lives are lost over these things," he said. [[c7]] On Monday, Sens. Jeanne Shaheen, Christopher A. Coons, Sheldon Whitehouse and Blumenthal, all Democrats, wrote to SpaceX asking for an explanation of the reported scaling back of Starlink and Starshield support to Ukraine. [[c25]]

The administration disputes the satellite account. Administration officials, including Trump, have denied throttling the service, Roll Call reports. [[c13]] Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on Oct. 17 that the administration had "nothing to do with that," and on Monday Trump said he did not know who ordered the interruption "but I'd like to find out," CBS News reported. [[c14]] Elon Musk wrote on X that Starshield systems are "owned and controlled by the US government" and that limits on speed or usage are decided by the military "and ultimately POTUS." [[c15]]

Trump has maintained his position. "I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don't want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table," he wrote on social media on Sunday. [[c26]] On Monday he told reporters on the South Lawn: "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine, they haven't been doing much." [[c27]] CBS News reports that the administration is under intense pressure to bring down fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections. [[c28]] Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said: "By giving the Russian economy life support, Trump's deal with the devil keeps getting dirtier." [[c38]]
whyItMatters: The law itself provides the waiver power. Section 115 of the law (Public Law 119-111) lets the President waive its sanctions, restrictions or duties after certifying to Congress in writing that the waiver is in the national interests of the United States and sending a report. [[c2]] The Oct. 16 order invokes that power and states that the certification has been submitted. [[c1]] The waivers stay in effect until the President or the Secretary of State decides further action is appropriate. [[c37]]

Some lawmakers link the waiver to the post-election session. Roll Call reports that a handful of Ukraine's Republican allies, joining most Democrats, are promising obstacles for the President's post-election agenda if the perceived tilt toward Moscow continues. [[c35]] Its analysis notes that with thin majorities in both chambers, it would not take many Republican defectors to threaten the NDAA and the Defense spending bills, among other measures. [[c29]] Bacon put the threat in writing on Oct. 17: "Many of us won't fund these things knowing he is propping up a dictator's invasion and throwing an ally under the bus." [[c17]] In that post he listed the President's agenda as "supplemental, reconciliation, Ballroom, etc." [[c18]] Not every critic accepts that link: Turner said he does not think "any brinkmanship" over the agenda is needed to change Russia policy. [[c8]]

Fitzpatrick's Oct. 10 remark refers to the House discharge rule. As described by the Congressional Research Service, it lets a measure reach the floor without committee action or leadership scheduling once 218 members, a majority, sign a petition; the motion can then be offered only after at least seven legislative days and only on the second or fourth Monday of a month. [[c31]] CRS also notes that these waiting periods let the Rules Committee preempt a discharge attempt by getting an alternative special rule adopted. [[c32]] On Oct. 15, 17 Democrats and five Republicans, among them Bacon, Fitzpatrick and McCaul, wrote Trump urging him to implement the Graham law's sanctions, according to Roll Call. [[c30]]
whatsNext: No Senate floor business is scheduled before the election. The Senate is holding only pro forma sessions with no business expected, the next on Oct. 22, and returns for business on Nov. 9. [[c33]] The Straits Times, carrying a Bloomberg story, says that with Congress out of session through the midterms there is little prospect of immediate action to block Trump's Russian diesel deal. [[c36]]

After Nov. 9, the pressure points are the must-pass bills Roll Call names, the NDAA and Defense spending, and the general funding deadline: under Public Law 119-103, current government funding expires on Dec. 11. [[c29]] [[c34]]
background: This story continues the editions of Oct. 17 and Oct. 18. On Oct. 16 Trump signed an executive order under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 (H.R. 5334, Public Law 119-111) waiving its sanctions, restrictions and duties, and stating that the national-interest certification required by the law had been sent to Congress. [[c1]] The Oct. 17 edition explained which sections the order waives; the Oct. 18 edition covered the first Republican reactions and the senators' Oct. 13 letter on the separate Russian diesel deal.

Section 115 is the provision at issue: it allows a waiver of "any sanctions provision," restriction or duty under the title once the President sends Congress a written national-interest certification and a report explaining its basis. [[c2]] Many Democrats criticized the bill during the debate partly because they considered the waiver authority too broadly worded, Roll Call reports. [[c39]]

Starlink is the commercial satellite network owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, and Starshield is the military version built on the same network. [[c40]] Ukrainian officials began reporting difficulties with the system, which is used for communication and to control drones, last week, CBS News reported. [[c41]] On Oct. 15, nine senators from both parties asked the Pentagon inspector general to investigate the reported restrictions, according to Roll Call. [[c42]]

notable.headline: DOJ charges 28 in California with voting crimes
notable.sentence: The Justice Department charged 28 people in California with voting crimes and asked a federal court on an emergency basis to stop the state from processing ballots from certain voters on federal lists, NPR reports.

notable.headline: Saudi JDAM sale published; Markey resolution still in committee
notable.sentence: The Federal Register on Oct. 19 published a proposed $5.0 billion sale of JDAM guidance kits and bombs to Saudi Arabia (Transmittal 26-35), which the notice says was delivered to Congress on Sept. 1; Sen. Edward J. Markey's disapproval resolution, S.J.Res. 216, has sat in the Foreign Relations Committee since Sept. 16.

notable.headline: More arms-sales notifications in the Federal Register
notable.sentence: The same Oct. 19 Federal Register issue carried further arms-sales notifications for Spain, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Jordan and the Netherlands, including $750 million in AGT-1500 tank engines for Saudi Arabia; no disapproval resolutions have been filed against these.

notable.headline: Texas Senate race close to tied in CBS News poll
notable.sentence: A CBS News poll finds the Texas Senate race between James Talarico and Ken Paxton close to tied, according to a CBS News video report that does not give the margin in its summary.

notable.headline: Midterm fundraising passes $15 billion
notable.sentence: More than $15 billion has been raised in this year's midterm elections, which could make them the most expensive on record, NPR reports.

notable.headline: Suspicious letters sent to election officials and congressional offices
notable.sentence: Federal investigators are examining suspicious letters containing unknown substances sent to state election officials and congressional offices, CBS News reports.

notable.headline: Hegseth meets Netanyahu on unannounced visit
notable.sentence: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on an unannounced visit amid reports of a possible restart of the Iran war, CBS News reports; no new war-powers measure has been filed.
